title: CAP & PACELC
subtitle: Cut the link between two replicas and watch the system be forced to choose between answering and being right.
learn: What CAP really says: during a network partition you give up consistency or availability
Why partitions are a fact of life, not an option you can decline
How PACELC adds the everyday trade-off: latency versus consistency when nothing is broken
The difference between strong, causal, and eventual consistency, with examples
How to pick a model per feature instead of per whole system

steps.title: Two copies of one value
steps.body: Imagine a setting x stored on two servers, called replicas: A in the US and B in Europe, so each user reads from a nearby copy. Both hold x = 4. Alice (US) sets x = 5 on A. A moment later, Bob (Europe) reads x from B. What should Bob see? And what if the link between A and B is cut right now?
steps.idea: Copying data to two places raises a question: which copy is allowed to be behind?
steps.caption: Alice's write reaches A; B still holds x = 4.

steps.title: Healthy network: easy
steps.body: The link is healthy, so A copies x = 5 to B and waits for B's "got it" (an acknowledgement, or ack) before telling Alice it worked. Now a read from either replica returns 5. This is strong consistency: the system acts as if there were only one copy. The cost is time. Alice waits for a round trip across the Atlantic, about 80 ms, on top of 5 ms for the local write: 85 ms in total.
steps.idea: With a healthy network you can have both consistency and availability. You just pay for it in latency.
steps.caption: A copies to B and waits for the ack before replying to Alice.

steps.title: The link breaks
steps.body: Now a cut cable or a bad router setting breaks the path between the regions. Both replicas are still running and both users can reach their nearest one, but A and B cannot talk to each other. This is a network partition. Neither side can tell whether the other has crashed or is just unreachable. Any system spread across a network will eventually see one, so you cannot design partitions away.
steps.idea: You do not get to choose whether partitions happen. CAP is about what you do once one does.
steps.caption: A and B are both up, but the link between them is down.

steps.title: Option 1: stay correct, refuse
steps.body: Option 1 puts correctness first. Such a system is called CP (consistent, partition-tolerant). A cannot be sure B will ever see the write, so it rejects Alice's request with an error (a 503, as the animation shows). B likewise refuses reads it cannot prove are current. Nobody sees stale or conflicting data, but users get errors while the partition lasts. Real CP systems with three or more replicas keep serving on the side that still has a majority. Only the minority side stops.
steps.idea: Choosing consistency means some requests fail for as long as the partition lasts.
steps.caption: A returns an error instead of accepting a write that B cannot see.

steps.title: Option 2: stay up, diverge
steps.body: Option 2 keeps the service up. Such a system is called AP (available, partition-tolerant). A accepts x = 5 and replies at once, because it does not wait for B. But Bob's read from B returns the old value 4. That answer is stale (out of date) but still valid, because B did respond. If Bob had also written x on B, the two copies would now disagree and must be reconciled later.
steps.idea: Choosing availability means the replicas can disagree while the partition lasts.
steps.caption: A accepts the write; B answers with the old value x = 4.

steps.title: The link comes back
steps.body: When the link comes back, an AP system has to catch up. A sends the missed update to B, and B applies it, so both hold 5 again. This is eventual consistency: if writes stop, all replicas end up equal. It promises the copies will agree, but not when. The hard case is two conflicting writes made on both sides. Deciding which one wins, or merging them, is covered in the clocks and CRDT lessons.
steps.idea: Eventual consistency promises the copies will converge, but not when, and not which conflicting write survives.
steps.caption: A pushes the missed write to B, and the copies match again.

steps.title: Even with no partition
steps.body: CAP only describes failures, but partitions are rare while the trade-off is constant. PACELC (say "pass-elk") extends it: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. That gives combinations such as PA/EL (favour uptime and speed) and PC/EC (favour correctness), plus the mixed PA/EC and PC/EL. The "Else" half matters most day to day, because every request pays it. Here, Alice waits for B's ack on every write.
steps.idea: PACELC: the everyday price of consistency is latency, paid even when nothing is broken.
steps.caption: Synchronous replication: Alice waits for B's ack.

steps.title: Else: pick latency
steps.body: The alternative is asynchronous replication. A confirms to Alice after its own 5 ms write, then sends x = 5 to B in the background. Writes become 17 times faster (5 ms instead of 85 ms). The price is that for roughly the next 40 ms (one way across the Atlantic), or longer under load, Bob can still read 4. Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra and Riak lean PA/EL by default, though quorum settings can shift that (see the Quorums lesson). Google Spanner is usually classed as PC/EC.
steps.idea: Async replication buys speed by letting replicas lag briefly. Sync replication buys correctness with delay.
steps.caption: A replies at once and copies to B in the background.

steps.title: A ladder of consistency
steps.body: Consistency comes in levels. Strong (linearizable): every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy. Causal: if one event could have influenced another, everyone sees them in that order. Example: Alice posts a question and Bob replies, so nobody may see the reply before the question. Eventual: copies only converge over time, with no ordering promise. Weaker levels are cheaper and faster. Causal can even stay available during a partition, since it needs ordering information, not agreement on every write.
steps.idea: Pick the weakest level your feature can tolerate. Causal adds ordering bookkeeping; strong adds cross-replica coordination.
steps.caption: Causal order: B must hold the post before showing the reply.

steps.title: How to think about it
steps.body: CAP: when a partition splits the replicas, choose consistency (reject some requests) or availability (accept requests and let copies diverge). It is not "pick two of three", because partitions will happen. PACELC: even with no partition, choose latency or consistency. Decide per feature. A bank balance and a unique username need strong consistency. A like counter or a feed can be eventual.
steps.idea: Ask two questions: what happens during a partition, and what latency do I pay when things are healthy?
steps.caption: All four parts: clients, two replicas, and the link between.

quiz.q: A three-replica database splits into a group of 2 and a lone replica. The lone replica rejects all writes. In CAP terms, what did the system choose?
options: Availability on every node
Consistency, giving up availability on the minority side
It gave up partition tolerance
Neither; this is not a CAP situation
quiz.why: Refusing writes that cannot be safely replicated preserves a single history (consistency) at the cost of the isolated node being unavailable. This is the CP choice.

quiz.q: A teammate says: 'We chose CA, so we never have to worry about partitions.' What is the flaw?
options: CA systems cannot have more than one replica
Availability is impossible without partition tolerance
CAP only applies to NoSQL databases
Network partitions happen regardless; you only decide how the system behaves when one occurs
quiz.why: On any real network, partitions happen whether you plan for them or not. A 'CA' design just has undefined or accidental behavior when one occurs.

quiz.q: Cross-region round trip is 80 ms. A service with no failures at all still sees 80 ms added to every write. Which idea explains this?
options: PACELC's 'else' branch: consistency costs latency even when healthy
The C in CAP, applied during partitions
Eventual consistency
Causal ordering
quiz.why: Waiting for a distant replica to acknowledge is the latency price of strong consistency, paid on every write even without a partition.

quiz.q: In a social app, Bob sees a reply to Alice's comment but not the comment itself. Which guarantee would prevent this?
options: Eventual consistency
Read-your-writes only for the commenter
Causal consistency
A longer replication timeout
quiz.why: Causal consistency ensures that if one event could have caused another, every reader sees them in that order. Plain eventual consistency allows the reply to arrive first.

quiz.q: Which feature most clearly needs strong consistency rather than eventual?
options: View count on a video
Claiming a unique username at signup
Number of followers shown on a profile
Recently viewed items list
quiz.why: Two replicas accepting the same username concurrently would break uniqueness. Counters and recency lists tolerate being briefly stale.

cheatsheet.def: During a network partition, a replicated system can keep consistency or availability, not both. Partitions are not optional.
Linearizability: every read returns the latest completed write, as if there were a single copy. Not the same as ACID consistency.
Every non-failing node answers every request with a non-error response, even if the data is stale.
If Partition: Availability or Consistency; Else: Latency or Consistency. Captures the everyday cost of strong guarantees.
Reads see the latest write. Needs coordination between replicas, so it costs round trips and can reject requests in a partition.
Related events (a question and its reply) are seen in order by everyone; unrelated events may appear in any order.
If writes stop, replicas converge. No promise about when, or about reads in the meantime. Fast and highly available.
Choose consistency per feature: money, uniqueness, and inventory lean strong; counters, feeds, and caches lean eventual.
